transcript.content: Hello, welcome to the clinic. What brings you in to see me today?

Well, my doctor thought I should come talk to someone because she seems worried my meal planning has gotten a little too… tight, I guess. I don’t really see it that way. I’ve always liked things orderly—my work was operations research, so measuring and planning doesn’t feel strange to me.

Mostly I just keep breakfast simple, like yogurt, and if I’m busy I might skip lunch, and then dinner is measured out so the day doesn’t get away from me. It feels sensible, but apparently she thinks it’s become a concern.
Do you ever feel anxious or upset if you can't stick to your meal plan?

I suppose I get a little unsettled if the plan changes, yes, but I wouldn’t call it dramatic. It’s more that I like the day to have a structure. Breakfast is usually just yogurt, and if I’m busy I may skip lunch—honestly when I was working in operations research, you learn to appreciate systems that don’t have too many variables.

Dinner is where I’m more careful, I guess. I measure things out so it doesn’t all get away from me. My doctor seems to think that’s too tight, but to me it mostly feels orderly.
Does your meal planning have anything to do with trying to control your weight?

I mean… yes, I suppose it does, at least partly. I don’t like saying it that way because it sounds vain or irrational, and I’m not trying to be difficult.

But if I’ve had a normal dinner, or especially if I eat out somewhere—restaurants always use so much oil, you know, and the portions are never consistent—then if the scale is up even a pound the next morning, I feel this sharp panic. Like I’ve lost control somehow. And then I feel like I need to correct it the next day, tighten things back up.
Do you have any other daily routines or habits that you feel compelled to follow very strictly?

I’m not sure, honestly. I mean, I’ve always had routines—most people do, don’t they? I like my kitchen put back a certain way and I keep lists, but that’s just… how I’ve always managed things. When I worked, if you didn’t track details, things fell apart, so maybe I carried some of that with me.

But compelled, strictly… I don’t know. Nothing is coming to mind the way the food planning does. I might be missing what you mean by habits, though.
Do you have recurring thoughts or ideas that you feel compelled to think about over and over?

Recurring thoughts… I’m not sure. I mean, I do think things through more than once, but I always thought that was just being careful. In operations research, you don’t just accept the first answer—you check the assumptions, run it again, see if there’s some variable you missed.

But compelled to think something over and over… I don’t know that I’d describe it that way. Maybe I’m not quite understanding what you mean by “ideas.” Are you asking about worries, or more like a phrase getting stuck in your head? Because I don’t think I have anything like that, not that I’ve really noticed.
Is your goal with meal planning to maintain a specific weight or avoid gaining weight?

I suppose it’s more about not gaining, if I’m being honest. I don’t have some official number written down or anything—well, I do notice the number, obviously—but it’s that if I’ve eaten a normal dinner, or gone to a restaurant, the next morning I’ll check and if it’s even up a pound I get this awful jolt of panic.

And I know scales fluctuate, I do know that. I used to deal with data, so I understand variation better than most people, probably. But in that moment it feels like I’ve let something slip, like I’ve lost control, and then I start planning how to correct it the next day. So… yes, avoiding gaining weight is part of it.
Do you have any recurring, intrusive thoughts that are not related to food or your weight?

Not that I can think of, no. I mean, my mind does wander—I’ll suddenly remember something I needed to put on a list, or I’ll think about whether I locked the back door, but I think that’s just normal, isn’t it? Especially as you get older, you start double-checking things because if you don’t write it down it disappears.

But recurring intrusive thoughts… not really, at least not outside the eating and weight stuff we were just talking about. Nothing that jumps out at me.
Do you feel compelled to perform any specific rituals or behaviors outside of your meal planning?

Rituals… outside of meals? I don’t think so. I mean, I have routines, certainly—at my age you sort of develop systems so you don’t spend half the day looking for your keys. I put the mail in the same spot, I make little lists, that sort of thing. When I was working, everything had a process, and I suppose some of that sticks with you.

But compelled, like I have to do it in a particular way or something terrible will happen… no, I don’t think I have anything like that. Not that I’ve noticed, anyway.
Do you think your need to measure out food and stick to your meal plan is more about keeping things orderly and controlled, or about preventing weight gain?

I suppose it’s a bit of both, though I tend to tell myself it’s about order. That’s sort of why I came in, really—my doctor seemed concerned that my meal planning had gotten too tight.

To me it just feels practical: breakfast is usually yogurt, then if I’m busy I might skip lunch, and dinner is measured out so the day doesn’t get away from me. I’ve always liked systems—when I was working, everything had to be organized or you’d miss something. But… yes, I can see that keeping it that controlled probably also has to do with not gaining weight.
When you think about not following your meal plan, what is it that you fear most: gaining weight or losing control of your daily routine?

I’d like to say it’s the routine, because that sounds more sensible, doesn’t it? I’ve always been someone who likes a plan. Even when I was working, if one number was off in a model, it could throw the whole thing, and I suppose I still think that way at home.

But if I’m being honest… it’s the weight. If I have a normal dinner, or we go to a restaurant and I can’t really measure things properly, and then the scale is up even a pound, I get this sharp sort of panic. Like I’ve lost control somehow, and then I feel I have to correct it the next day. So yes, I think gaining weight is what frightens me most, even if I dress it up as “keeping to the routine.”
When you imagine yourself at your ideal weight, do you think you would still feel the need to measure out your food so carefully?

I suppose… I probably would, yes. Though I’m not sure I think of it as “ideal weight,” exactly. That phrase makes me think of charts at the doctor’s office, and those never seemed very personal, did they? When I was doing operations work, we always had targets and ranges, but real life is messier than a spreadsheet.

But yes, the measuring—I think I’d still do it, because to me it feels like keeping the day orderly. That’s really why I came in, because my doctor thought my meal planning had gotten too tight. I just think of it as yogurt for breakfast, maybe no lunch if I’m busy, and then a very measured dinner so things don’t get away from me. It feels sensible to me, though I suppose the fact that it feels necessary is what worries everyone.
Do you think you would still feel anxious if you gained a small amount of weight but were able to maintain your daily routine and structure?

Yes… I think I would. I mean, I could have the whole day perfectly arranged—breakfast as planned, errands in the right order, dinner measured out—and if the scale were up even a pound, especially after something like a normal dinner or eating out, I’d still feel this sudden panic.

It’s funny, because in my old work we used to say a small variation wasn’t necessarily meaningful—you had to look at the trend, not one data point. But when it’s me, I don’t seem to treat it that way. It feels like I’ve let something slip, and then I start thinking I need to make up for it the next day. So yes, even with the routine intact, the weight change would still upset me.
Do you think you could ever stop measuring your food portions if you felt secure that your weight would remain stable?

Maybe… if I really believed that. But I’m not sure I know how to feel secure about it without checking and measuring, if that makes sense.

I mean, the reason I came in is because my doctor thinks my meal planning has gotten too tight. To me it just feels orderly—yogurt for breakfast, then if I’m busy I might not bother with lunch, and dinner is measured so the day doesn’t get away from me. It’s like when I used to keep spreadsheets balanced; once you stop tracking things, you don’t really know where you are.

So I suppose I’d like to say yes, I could stop measuring, but honestly I think it would be very hard. Measuring is sort of how I make myself feel secure in the first place.
Is your anxiety about weight gain more about the actual weight or how it makes you feel about yourself?

I think it’s more how it makes me feel about myself, though I suppose the actual weight is the number I latch onto. It’s… the number is like the signal that something is wrong.

I know I’m not a young woman trying to fit into some magazine idea—goodness, at my age I’m not trying to look twenty-five again. But I still find myself judging whether I’m handling things properly by how my waist and hips look in my clothes. If they feel contained, if my clothes sit right, then I feel more… in control, I guess.

It’s funny, I used to be very practical about clothing—good seams, washable fabrics, pockets if you could find them, which is nearly impossible in women’s clothes—but now I notice whether things feel snug in those areas, and it affects how I see the whole day. So yes, it’s not just the pounds. It’s what I think they say about me.
Is your desire to control your food intake more about preventing weight gain or about feeling in control of your life in general?

I suppose it’s a little of both, but I think I tell myself it’s about keeping life orderly. My doctor is the one who seems concerned that my meal planning has gotten too tight, but to me it just feels… sensible, I guess.

I’ll have yogurt for breakfast, and if I’m busy I may skip lunch without really thinking much of it, and then dinner is very measured so the day doesn’t sort of spread out all over the place. It reminds me of scheduling work—though, I suppose that’s not exactly the same thing, is it? But there’s a comfort in knowing what’s coming and not having to make too many decisions.

So yes, preventing weight gain is part of it, but the way it feels to me day-to-day is more like keeping everything in its proper place.
Is your strict meal planning something you think you could relax if you didn't have to worry about your weight at all?

If I truly didn’t have to worry about my weight at all? Maybe I could relax it some, but I’m not sure I know how to separate the two.

I mean, I came in because my doctor thinks my meal planning has gotten too tight, though to me it feels more like keeping things orderly. Yogurt for breakfast, and if I’m busy I might just not stop for lunch—though that happens with paperwork too, you know, you look up and the afternoon’s gone—and then dinner is measured so the day doesn’t get away from me.

So I suppose if weight weren’t a worry, maybe the measuring would feel less necessary. But part of me would still want the structure. It’s hard to imagine just… eating without a plan.
Do you think you would still feel the need to control your food intake if you were at a weight that you considered ideal?

I think… probably yes, at least some. If I were at what I thought was the right weight, I’d still want the routine, because that’s what keeps the day from feeling loose around the edges.

I know my doctor seems concerned that my meal planning has gotten too tight, but to me it just feels practical—yogurt for breakfast, and if I’m busy I might skip lunch, and then dinner is very measured. It’s almost like how I used to organize reports at work—everything in its place, nothing left dangling. Though I suppose food isn’t exactly a spreadsheet, is it?

So yes, even at an ideal weight, I think I’d still feel pulled to keep it controlled. Maybe not as nervously, but I’d still want it orderly.
Do you think you would still feel the need to measure your food portions if you were confident that you could maintain your current weight without doing so?

I think I’d still measure, yes… though maybe I’d tell myself it was just habit, not worry.

I came in because my doctor seems concerned that my meal planning has gotten too tight, but to me it feels like keeping the day from getting messy. Yogurt for breakfast, and if I’m busy I don’t always stop for lunch—though that happens with all sorts of things, I used to do that with spreadsheets too, just lose track—and then dinner is very measured. It makes the evening feel settled, I suppose.

So even if I knew my weight would stay the same, I think I’d still want the portions measured. It’s less… dramatic that way. Everything stays orderly.
Is your strict meal planning primarily a way to prevent weight gain or a way to feel more in control of your daily life?

I suppose it’s more about control… though I don’t know that I’d put it that starkly. Weight is in there somewhere, of course, but I came in because my doctor thinks my meal planning has gotten too tight, and to me it mostly feels like keeping the day orderly.

Breakfast is just yogurt, which is easy, and then if I’m busy I might not stop for lunch—honestly that used to happen when I was working on models too, you just keep adjusting one little thing and suddenly it’s late—and then dinner is measured so there aren’t any surprises.

So… yes, maybe it prevents things from getting away from me, but not just weight. More like the whole day.
Is your strict meal planning something you think you could stop doing if you felt completely in control of other aspects of your life?

I’m not sure I could just stop, even if everything else felt perfectly under control. I mean, in theory maybe I’d loosen it a bit, but… the meal planning has become part of how I keep the day in order.

I came in because my doctor seems concerned it’s gotten too tight, though to me it doesn’t feel dramatic. It’s just yogurt in the morning, and if I’m busy I might skip lunch, and then dinner is very measured. It reminds me a little of how I used to structure my workday—if one part was predictable, the rest felt less likely to go off track.

So if other parts of my life felt controlled, maybe I’d have less reason to lean on it, but I don’t know that I’d stop. It feels like its own kind of order now.
